{{Short description|Concept used in black hole solutions}}
Closed trapped surfaces are a concept used in black hole solutions of [[general relativity]]<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Senovilla|first1=Jose M. M.|title=Trapped Surfaces|date=September 15, 2011|arxiv=1107.1344|doi=10.1142/S0218271811020354|volume=20|issue=11|journal=International Journal of Modern Physics D|pages=2139–2168|bibcode=2011IJMPD..20.2139S|s2cid=119249809}}</ref> which describe the inner region of an [[event horizon]]. [[Roger Penrose]] defined the notion of closed trapped surfaces in 1965.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Penrose|first1=Roger|title=Gravitational collapse and space-time singularities|journal=Phys. Rev. Lett.|date=January 1965|volume=14|issue=3|pages=57–59|doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.14.57|bibcode = 1965PhRvL..14...57P |doi-access=free}}</ref> A trapped surface is one where light is not moving away from the black hole. The boundary of the union of all trapped surfaces around a black hole is called an [[apparent horizon]].

A related term [[trapped null surface]] is often used interchangeably. However, when discussing [[Causal patch|causal horizons]], trapped null surfaces are defined as only null vector fields giving rise to null surfaces. But marginally trapped surfaces may be spacelike, timelike or null.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Nielsen|first1=Alex B.|title=Revisiting Vaidya Horizons|journal=Galaxies|date=February 10, 2014|volume=2|issue=1|pages=62–71|doi=10.3390/galaxies2010062|bibcode = 2014Galax...2...62N |doi-access=free}}</ref>

==Definition==

They are [[Spacetime#Spacetime interval|spacelike]] surfaces (topological spheres, tubes, etc.) with restricted bounds, their area tending to decrease locally along any possible future direction and with a dual definition with respect to the past. The trapped surface is a spacelike surface of co-dimension 2, in a [[Pseudo-Riemannian manifold|Lorentzian spacetime]]. It follows<ref>{{cite arXiv|last1=Bengtsson|first1=Ingemar|title=Some Examples of Trapped Surfaces|date=December 22, 2011|eprint=1112.5318|class=gr-qc}}</ref> that any [[normal bundle|normal vector]] can be expressed as a linear combination of two future directed null vectors, normalised by:
<math display=block>
k_+\cdot k_-=-2
</math>
The <math>k_+</math> vector is directed "outwards" and <math>k_-</math> "inwards". The set of all such vectors engenders one outgoing and one ingoing null congruence. The surface is designated trapped if the cross sections of both congruences decrease in area as they exit the surface; and this is apparent in the mean curvature vector, which is:
<math display=block>
H^\alpha=-\theta_+k_-^\alpha-\theta_-k_+^\alpha
</math>
The surface is trapped if both the null expansions <math>\theta_\pm</math> are negative, signifying that the mean curvature vector is timelike and future directed. The surface is marginally trapped if the outer expansion <math>\theta_+=0</math> and the inner expansion <math>\theta_-\le 0</math>.

==Trapped null surface==
A '''trapped null surface''' is a [[Set (mathematics)|set]] of points defined in the context of [[general relativity]] as a closed surface on which outward-pointing [[ray (optics)|light ray]]s are actually converging (moving inwards).

Trapped null surfaces are used in the definition of the [[apparent horizon]] which typically surrounds a [[black hole]].

===Definition===
We take a ([[Compact space|compact]], [[Orientability|orientable]], [[Spacetime#Spacetime interval|spacelike]]) surface, and find its outward pointing [[Surface normal|normal]] vectors.  The basic picture to think of here is a ball with pins sticking out of it; the pins are the normal vectors.

Now we look at light rays that are directed outward, along these normal vectors.  The rays will either be diverging (the usual case one would expect) or converging.  Intuitively, if the light rays are converging, this means that the light is moving backwards inside of the ball.  If all the rays around the entire surface are converging, we say that there is a '''trapped null surface'''.

More formally, if every null congruence orthogonal to a spacelike two-surface has negative expansion, then such surface is said to be trapped.
